title: unique_ptr and Move: Handing Ownership Over

questions.question: What is the difference between copying and moving?
options: A copy makes a second independent object, a move transfers what the object holds and leaves the source empty
There is no difference for class types
A move is a faster copy
A move destroys the source object
questions.explanation: For a resource, moving is the right operation: there is still exactly one device or file or lock, and only the owner changed.

questions.question: What does std::move actually do?
options: It allocates a new object and frees the old one
Nothing at run time, it is a cast saying this object may be taken from
It destroys the original object
It copies the object to a new location
questions.explanation: The transfer is performed by the type's move constructor or move assignment. The name is misleading and worth saying out loud once.

questions.question: What may you do with an object after moving from it?
options: Nothing at all, touching it is undefined behaviour
Anything, it is unchanged
Assign a new value to it, or let it be destroyed
Only read from it
questions.explanation: It is valid but empty, and its destructor will still run. Its value is not something to rely on, but it is safe to reassign or destroy.

questions.question: What does a parameter of type std::unique_ptr<Device> tell a reader?
options: The function will look at the device without keeping it
The function is taking ownership: give it to me, it is mine now
The device might be null
The function will make a copy of the device
questions.explanation: Ownership appears in the signature and the compiler enforces it, so a reader knows who owns what without reading the body.

questions.question: Why does take move the pointer out of the vector before erasing that slot?
options: Because vectors cannot hold unique_ptr
Because erase invalidates the id
Erasing would destroy the device it is trying to hand over
To keep the vector sorted
questions.explanation: The vector owns the device until the ownership is moved out. Erasing first would run the destructor and leave nothing to return.

questions.question: Why does find return a raw Device* rather than a unique_ptr?
options: Because raw pointers are faster
Because the device might not exist
Because unique_ptr cannot be returned
The caller is looking without taking, and a raw pointer says exactly that
questions.explanation: Returning a unique_ptr would mean handing over ownership. A non owning raw pointer is the correct spelling of look but do not keep.
